title: SMTP Service Extension for 8-bit MIME Transport
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets message bodies with octets outside US-ASCII be relayed directly. It obsoletes RFC 1652 and is a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: 8BITMIME lets an SMTP client send a MIME body containing octets outside the US-ASCII range when the server advertises support. The server must preserve the data, but the extension does not carry unencoded binary content.

questions: what does body=8bitmime do in smtp
what happens if a server does not support 8bitmime
subtitle: How SMTP negotiates support for MIME message bodies containing 8-bit data.

tldr.problem: SMTP was designed for 7-bit US-ASCII, while MIME messages may contain octets outside that range.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises the 8BITMIME keyword in its EHLO response. A client then identifies the message body with BODY=8BITMIME on the MAIL command.
tldr.outcome: A supporting server must preserve every bit, but line-length limits still apply and BINARY content-transfer-encoding is not supported. RFC 6152 obsoletes RFC 1652.

today: RFC 6152 is Internet Standard 71 and obsoletes RFC 1652. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SMTP Needs 8BITMIME
sections.content:
SMTP systems wanted to exchange MIME message bodies containing octets outside the US-ASCII range. RFC 6152 defines an extension to SMTP for transporting that content.

The extension does not remove SMTP line-length restrictions. A server may still enforce a line limit no lower than 1000 octets, so this is not a way to transfer unencoded binary data.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP can use this extension for MIME bodies containing 8-bit data. It still has line-length limits and does not carry arbitrary binary files as-is.

sections.title: The Extension Parameters
sections.content:
The extension is named 8bit-MIMEtransport, and its EHLO keyword is 8BITMIME. The keyword has no parameter, and the extension adds no SMTP verbs.

The extension adds an optional BODY parameter to MAIL. Its value is 7BIT for a message that follows SMTP's 7-bit requirements or 8BITMIME for a MIME message containing arbitrary octet-aligned material.
sections.plainLanguage: The server advertises 8BITMIME in EHLO. The sender then labels the MAIL command with BODY=7BIT or BODY=8BITMIME to describe the message body.

sections.title: Negotiating and Sending 8-bit Content
sections.content:
A client first sends EHLO. If the server replies with code 250 and includes 8BITMIME, it is saying that it accepts the extended MAIL command. The client must include one BODY parameter when it sends the message.

A supporting server must preserve every bit in each octet accepted through DATA. SMTP dot-stuffing still applies, and the CR-LF before the terminating dot is part of the message body. Line-length restrictions still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks the server's EHLO response before sending an 8-bit body. If the server advertises support, it must preserve the message octets it accepts.

sections.title: When the Server Does Not Advertise Support
sections.content:
If the server does not return code 250 to EHLO or does not include 8BITMIME, a client MUST NOT send content containing octets outside the US-ASCII range.

The client can convert the message to valid 7-bit MIME without losing information, or treat the unsupported transfer as a permanent delivery error. The RFC does not define the conversion procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Without an 8BITMIME advertisement, the client cannot send the 8-bit body. It can convert the message to 7-bit MIME without information loss or report a delivery failure.

sections.title: Example SMTP Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC's example begins with an EHLO request and a server reply that includes 8BITMIME. The client then sends MAIL FROM with BODY=8BITMIME, specifies a recipient, and transmits the message with DATA.

The server accepts the message after the client ends the DATA transfer with the SMTP terminator.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows the server advertising support before the client sends a message marked BODY=8BITMIME. The client then transmits the message through the ordinary DATA command.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not identify new security issues beyond those already present in conforming SMTP and email systems. Because MIME semantics do not depend on the transport encoding, 8BITMIME does not add a new ability to spread malware compared with 7-bit SMTP.

IANA updated the SMTP service-extension registry entry for 8BITMIME to refer to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says 8BITMIME does not add security concerns beyond those already associated with email. IANA updated the registry entry for the extension.
